//: TRI-RUNTIME BEHAVIOURAL FIXTURE for the maneuver-planner command surface. Every case here is byte-diffed across the browser harness, native WasmEdge and the pinned Docker WasmEdge, at 1/2/4/8 threads. Success paths AND failure paths: a deterministic error is parity evidence exactly like a deterministic answer. Until 0.2.0 this module's failure path was a TRAP (its exceptions were compiled out) and the cases below expected the trap CLASS to match across lanes. 0.2.0 gave the module a real error path, so those same cases now expect "guest-error" — the SAME inputs, judged by the same instrument, with the expectation flipped in the commit that flipped the behaviour. Run: space-data-module parity --wasm dist/isomorphic/module.wasm --fixture parity/maneuver-command.json --lanes browser,wasmedge,docker-wasmedge
name: maneuver-command-parity

cases.//: The canonical case the program pins. Also the tightest possible parity probe: a closed-form answer that is a handful of sqrt() calls, so any divergence between lanes is a libm difference and nothing else.

Positive phase angle: the phasing orbit is SMALLER and the first burn is retrograde. The response carries only the magnitude, so what this case pins across lanes is that phasingSMA — the quantity the console wrapper recovers the sign from — is byte-identical everywhere.

170 degrees in one revolution. 0.1.0 returned a phasing orbit whose far apse was ~4,300 km BENEATH the surface, with no error and no flag, and this case existed to pin that the DEFECT was reproduced identically on all three runtimes so the console-side guard was known to be guarding the same behaviour everywhere. 0.2.0 clamps to Re+100 km and says so (clampedToEarthFloor, farApse, achievedPhaseAngle), so what is pinned now is the GUARD: the clamp must fire at the same input and produce the same numbers on every lane.

Tudat's elliptical Lambert case. In 0.1.0 this was the one geometry the solver got right, included so the parity lane would already be watching the operation when the defect was repaired. It is repaired: solveLambert is a bracketed, residual-checked universal-variable solve and all four Tudat rows arrive. This case now also pins `converged` and `residual`, which are measurements rather than the literal `true` 0.1.0 returned on every path.

THE 0.3.0 BRACKETING REPAIR, as a parity case. Curtis example 5.3: the zero-revolution root sits at z = -0.173 inside a domain that ends at z = -0.398, so 0.2.0 stepped over it and answered no-solution on every lane. It is here because the repair is a SEARCH change — the one class of change whose answer can legitimately differ between two libm implementations if a probe lands on the boundary differently — and a search that brackets identically on three runtimes is the evidence that it does not.

The multi-revolution HIGH branch (0.3.0). Der Molniya, one revolution, second sign change — an arc no version through 0.2.0 could return. The scan that finds it walks 2048 nodes and counts sign changes, so a single node classified differently on one lane would return the OTHER arc, and that difference is 1.03 km/s of departure speed rather than a last-digit wobble.
The same geometry with NO branch stated: the default must still be the low arc, byte for byte, on every lane. Paired with the case above, this is what pins the selector without loosening the default.

The transfer-conic report on a HYPERBOLIC arc (0.3.0): perigeeRadius, transferEccentricity and transferConic present, apogeeRadius ABSENT because the arc never returns. The conditional key is the part worth diffing across lanes — a lane that emitted it, or omitted transferSemiMajorAxis, would be serving a different contract from the same bytes.

solveLambertMinDV over both branches (0.3.0), on a geometry where the high branch wins by a factor of thirty-six. The response carries the whole candidate set it ranked, so this case diffs an ORDERED COMPOSITE across lanes rather than a scalar: same members, same order, same costs.

A refusal is parity evidence exactly like an answer, and it is filed as expect:"ok" for the same reason every other refusal case in this fixture is — the class describes whether the INVOKE completed, and a structured error did complete; what is byte-diffed is the error frame itself. The branch selector admits two names and no third; a lane that fell back to the default instead of refusing would hand a caller a different arc than the one it asked for, silently.

An unknown operation returns errorCode "unknown-operation" and a JSON {error, errorCode} body, identically on every lane. Under 0.1.0 this aborted the guest and poisoned the instance. EXIT CLASS IS "ok", NOT "guest-error": the command surface always exits 0 and encodes the refusal INTO the PIV response envelope ({error, errorCode} plus the module's message). That makes "ok" the stronger expectation here, because an "ok" case is additionally BYTE-DIFFED across every lane and thread count — so the whole error payload, message text included, is pinned rather than just the class. What changed at 0.2.0 is that this input used to produce class "trap".

cases.//: Below the JSON bridge entirely: the host codec's own rejection path, which must also agree across lanes.

An antipodal geometry: r1 and r2 exactly opposed, so every plane through the line is a valid transfer plane and no unique solution exists. The universal-variable formulation says so algebraically (A = 0). 0.1.0 answered converged:true here. The REFUSAL must be identical across lanes — a solver that refuses in one runtime and answers in another is the worst possible isomorphism failure, because the answer is the wrong one. 0.1.0 COMPUTED dv1_ric/dv2_ric/dv3_ric and aTransfer1/aTransfer2 for this operation and dropped all five at the JSON boundary, forcing the console to recover the burn signs from monotone comparisons. They are serialised now; this case byte-diffs the signed arrays across lanes, which is a stricter probe than the magnitudes were (a sign is one bit that either agrees or does not).
